vignette:
She is twenty years old and works as a pharmacist in a small community pharmacy in a city that feels both safe and foreign. Most mornings she arrives before the store opens, unlocks the heavy metal grate with trembling fingers, and takes three slow breaths before stepping inside. The fluorescent lights hum overhead, and the antiseptic smell of the pharmacy is familiar enough to anchor her—but only just.

The torture happened two years ago, in a country far from here. She was finishing her final year of pharmacy school when the soldiers came. They accused her of distributing medicines to people they called “enemies of the state.” In reality, she had simply filled a prescription for an elderly woman whose son was a known activist. The soldiers did not care about the distinction. They took her from the clinic, blindfolded her, and kept her in a windowless room for three days.

She remembers the sounds most clearly: the scrape of a chair on concrete, the metallic clink of a bucket being kicked across the floor, the voice of a man who spoke her own language but with a cold, practiced calm. They beat the soles of her feet with a rubber hose—falanga, they called it—until she could no longer stand. They burned the inside of her left forearm with a cigarette, the scar still a pale, puckered map beneath her white coat. They asked questions she could not answer, and when she did not answer, they hurt her again. On the third day, the international news covered a protest in the capital, and the soldiers grew distracted. She crawled out of a broken window as the sun was setting, her feet swollen, her mind blank.

She made it to a relative’s house, then to a refugee camp, then, through a series of improbable phone calls and false documents, to this city. Now she lives with her boyfriend, Kwame, a nursing student who never asks too many questions about her past. He is kind, patient, and sometimes that makes it worse. When he touches her shoulder unexpectedly, she flinches so hard she drops her coffee mug. She apologizes, picks up the shards, and says nothing else.

At work, she has learned to read the faces of customers. A man in a uniform—even a postal worker—makes her pulse race. She grips the counter until her knuckles whiten. Once, a customer laughed loudly, and she dropped a bottle of cough syrup, the glass shattering across the tile. Her manager said it was fine, but she could not stop shaking for an hour. She avoids the back storage room because it has no windows. She never takes her break in the staff lounge if the door is closed. She always leaves the bathroom door slightly ajar.

Sleep comes in fragments. Most nights she wakes at 3:00 a.m., her heart hammering, convinced she hears boots on the stairs. Kwame sleeps beside her, unaware of the vigil she keeps. She has not told him the full story. She does not know how to say that sometimes she still feels the rubber hose, that she cannot stand to have her feet touched, that she flinches when he takes his shoes off near her.

At the pharmacy counter, she fills prescriptions for antidepressants, antipsychotics, and sleep aids for others, but she has not filled one for herself. She is certain that if she stops being hypervigilant, something terrible will happen. She checks the locks on her apartment door three times before bed. She scans the faces of every man who enters the pharmacy. She is always ready to run, even though there is nowhere left to go.

Her boyfriend notices that she does not laugh the way she used to. She says she is tired. She says work is stressful. She does not tell him that she feels hollow, or that the only time she feels anything close to alive is when she counts pills in the quiet of the morning, her hands steady, her mind blank. The scar on her arm itches under her sleeve. She does not scratch it. She does not want to remember. But the body remembers for her, every single day.
